title: Brother Leonce's ear, his trumpet and funerals of old musicians
summary: Leonce learned by ear, refused to wear fancy dress, and never changed slides; Mello hasn't touched their trumpet since, and complains that white musicians' funerals draw few attendees.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Well, to get into Leonce's life a little, did he study music?

Yeah, with his ears. With his ears. I'll tell you what, not that he was my brother like I told Crawford. Not that he was my brother. But whatever the heck he put his hands on and he wanted to play, he played. And it didn't matter what he played, he used to go around the nigger bands and listen to the execution. Oh, he'd come home and play it. If he went to the niggers and heard one piece of music, he'd come home and play it. That's just how good a head he had. He could have gone on with Ted Lewis. Ted Lewis wanted he and I both. Leonce says that the only time they're gonna put a frock on him is when he's dead. He wouldn't use no white suit. And he positively wouldn't use no tuxedo. He would not. Uh-uh, Leonce is a queer sort of a doctor. But as queer as he was in music, you couldn't beat him. As good as he was, you couldn't beat him in music. Like I told Crawford, like I tell anybody else. You wanna see how good a musician is? Put him in a funeral and he's gonna play on a beat. Then you'll find out what kind of musician he is. But Leonce just had the knack. He had the head and he had the know-how. That's what you could call it, the know-how. Boy, he could play. He could play and he had a lip like that, that table, hard like that, like me. Now you've seen my trumpet. That trumpet ain't been used since Leonce died. Whenever I'm gonna play a trumpet, Jabba, Google, make a fire, eat it for my brother-law from the other fella down below. I don't know. I never touched that horn. Leonce and I played the last job with that horn. We played at a reception. That was about three years before he died. And just as the horn you see there, that's the way the horn's been set. Because the piano was in international pitch, high pitch. So naturally, you had to put on a high-pitched slide. So we put the high-pitched slide on and as you see that horn then, now, that's the way it was done. He was a good musician. And every time I play music, I always feel it. I got him on the side of me, but the trumpet ain't there. You come back behind you, ain't there at all. So I go out, but I feel worse when I go play music. I don't see if I'm playing around with a whole lot of noise and stuff. That's different. But to go play a real job, boy, that right-handed got him lost. I mean I'm lost. So I miss Leonce. And like I tell you, my horn been in that same position from the day Leonce. So the day we quit playing music, he quit playing. And I ain't touched on him since. Well, when did he die? He died five years ago. And Henry died two years later. I'll tell you, it's pitiful when you know fellas like that, anyhow, you catch a whole lot of fellas that thinks they're musicians. But I'll say this for Leonce, and I'll say it for Leonce again. Leonce never changed the slide on his trumpet. It didn't matter what key you played in. You could play in sharps or flats or any other key. He played. And he had it. But a lot of these fellas in the old days, when you're playing all right, what you're going to play, we're going to play flats. All right, wait, I'm going to put a flat-sized high-pitched slide on it. Now, if you want to play in sharps, he might make, he can play one or two keys in sharps, but he can't play the piece through. He can vamp on it. When you want to play in sharps, you got to wait until he took that phrase and slide out the end of his horn and put another one in. Bring his, lower the pitch on the horn. Not allowance, allowance to put a hang with color. What kind of frasslin' key you played in, he played. I don't care what it was. So, he was a good musician. Now, you take a lot of these niggas that die, and that's what binds me up. The Souchon Brigade, they, I'm not knocking now, but when the niggas died, everybody had to attend the niggas funerals. And when the white fellas died, it was as good or better than the niggas, they couldn't even, even if they wasn't half as good as the niggas. Nobody never showed up. Nobody never showed up. They didn't worry about that. I was just another musician. That's all. Papa Celestine, when Papa Celestine died, the whole frasin' jazz outfit had a possession behind him. When quite a few of the old times, Humpback Gallaty, he was one of the old-time musicians. Leonce was another one. Martin Kurch was another one. Gelo Nunes was another one. Quite a few of the old times, it was real musicians. Nobody had just died and got better than that was all. So, that's the only thing that I don't approve of.
Well, that generation is forgotten today, pretty much. I know.
